issues.legal_issue: A place used for public religious worship is a public temple and public trust when the evidence shows that the public or a section of it worships there as of right and the surrounding circumstances support dedication for the public’s benefit.
material_facts: The temple was ancient, and its origin was lost in antiquity; no reliable documentary evidence of dedication was available.
Large numbers of people from the Hindu community visited the temple for worship and to fulfil vows, without being prevented from visiting.
A restriction on entry and inside worship was treated as an arrangement for orderly darshan, rather than proof that public access was by permission only.
Rulers provided regular cash grants for the temple, and devotees made offerings and donated land and other property to the deity.
Government and revenue records showed temple property in the deity’s name, and historical records described the temple and public worship there.

The appellants’ family managed the temple and its properties, but that circumstance was not conclusive of private character; prior civil proceedings had not determined the temple’s public or private status.
issues.conclusion: The temple was a public temple and a public trust, and the High Court correctly upheld its registration as such.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(17) and 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, a temple is a place used for public religious worship and dedicated to, for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it; a public trust includes such a temple. The distinction is between specific, ascertainable beneficiaries of a private endowment and the general public or an indeterminate class benefiting from a public endowment. Dedication need not be documented and may be inferred from conduct and circumstances. Long use by the public as of right, public or royal grants and gifts, property held in the deity’s name, and the understanding of managers and worshippers are relevant; family management and internal arrangements for orderly worship are not conclusive. The Court applied Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwala v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi, Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S.P. Sahi, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Ranchhoddas Kalidas, State of Bihar v. Charusila Dasi, Bihar State Board of Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das, T.D. Gopalan v. Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Dhaneshwarbuwa Guru Purshottambuwa v. Charity Commissioner, T.V. Mahalinga Iyer v. State of Madras, Sri Radhakanta Deb v. Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Hari Bhanu Maharaj of Baroda v. Charity Commissioner, Jammi Raja Rao v. Sri Anjaneyaswami Temple Vahi, and Kapoor Chand v. Ganesh Dutt. The Court also held that the Bombay Presidency Gazette was admissible under sections 35 and 81 of the Evidence Act, 1872, and that its historical statements could be considered with other evidence, though they were not conclusive.

rule.if: public_trust_status_appeal and public_worship_as_right and (long_public_use or large_public_attendance) and (public_or_ruler_support or property_in_deity_name)

predicates.public_trust_status_appeal: A party appealed a determination about whether a religious site was a public trust.
predicates.public_worship_as_right: Members of the public or a section of the religious community used the site for worship as of right, rather than solely by individual permission.
predicates.long_public_use: The public or a section of it had used the site for worship over a long period.
predicates.large_public_attendance: Large numbers of members of the public or a religious community attended the site for worship.
predicates.public_or_ruler_support: Members of the public or rulers provided grants, offerings, donations, or other support for the site.
predicates.property_in_deity_name: Records showed that property associated with the site was held in the name of its deity.

issues.definition: When an appeal about a religious site’s trust status involves public worship as of right and the specified evidence of public use and support or deity-owned property, the site is a public trust.

issues.legal_issue: The public-trust status of other religious sites should not be determined without a fresh inquiry when the earlier joint inquiry produced prejudicial and lopsided results.
material_facts: The Assistant Charity Commissioner had conducted a joint inquiry concerning several temples and a Haveli.
The High Court found that the joint inquiry had produced prejudicial and lopsided results and directed a fresh inquiry concerning the other temples and the Haveli.
The Supreme Court considered it inappropriate to make findings on the status of those other sites in this appeal.
issues.conclusion: The direction for a fresh inquiry concerning the other temples and the Haveli was upheld, and the Court made no finding on their public or private status.
issues.legal_principle: The Court left the status of the other sites to a fresh inquiry because the earlier joint inquiry had produced prejudicial and lopsided results; it did not decide their status on the record before it.

predicates.appeal_involving_multiple_religious_site: A party appealed in a proceeding that concerned the status of multiple religious sites.
predicates.joint_inquiry_was_prejudicial_or_lopside: The earlier joint inquiry concerning the sites produced prejudicial or lopsided results.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns multiple religious sites and the joint inquiry produced prejudicial or lopsided results, a fresh inquiry is required for the other sites.
